edits.walkthrough_append: Worked check: trace one silsila's career — the Chishtis arrive in the late twelfth century, settle Ajmer and then Delhi, refuse state offices and gifts, and grow by the aura of their khanqahs; the Suhrawardis accept court posts and advise sultans. Two styles of power: proximity without office versus influence through office. For the board examination, Sufism-in-India answers define tasawwuf and silsila (the chain of initiation), name two orders with founders and localities, and close with the relation to the state — who took its money, who refused — since that choice is what made each order's history.

Worked check: read the order through one practice — the Chishti shaikh lives simply, eats what is given today, holds open audiences (majlis) where qalandars, peasants and amirs sit together, and declines the court's invitation; when the Sultan comes to the door, the shaikh rises but does not leave his khanqah. Muinuddin at Ajmer, Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki in Delhi, Nizamuddin Auliya in the Sultanate's storm — three generations of that stance. For the board examination, Chishti answers give the founder and locality, the moral economy (poverty, refusal of office, hospitality), one shaikh anecdote, and why the dargahs still draw millions.

Worked check: walk one visitor's day — he arrives at the dargah, makes the ziyarat (the visit to the tomb), offers the chadar; the qawwals sing the shaikh's sama in the courtyard, the music that carried the mystical verses; he eats from the langar cooked in the free kitchen that once fed Delhi's poor. Three practices, one institution. For the board examination, devotional-practice answers define ziyarat, sama and langar in a line each, place them in the khanqah's daily rhythm, and close with the social reading — the dargah as the one medieval space where classes and creeds met as equals.

Worked check: follow the prince's project — Dara Shukoh studies with Mulla Shah of the Qadiri order, learns Sanskrit with pandits, then publishes his comparative works: the Majma-ul-Bahrayn (the mingling of the two oceans) pairing Sufi and Vedantic terms, and the Sirr-i-Akbar, his Persian translation of the Upanishads, which he reads as the hidden scripture the Quran itself announces. A programme of unity, written before the succession war killed him. For the board examination, Dara questions give the translation project with dates, the two-ocean thesis in a line, and the historiographical point — his fate made him the symbol of a possible composite culture.

Worked check: assemble the rediscovery from its sources — Colonel Mackenzie collects manuscripts and early survey notes in 1800; others sketch the ruins; then in 1856 Alexander Greenlaw photographs the site in detail; long after, in the twentieth century, epigraphists read the royal orders and John Fritz and George Michell survey the city block by block. Texts, photographs and measured ruins agree on one city. For the board examination, rediscovery answers run this source-list in order with dates, and close on the method: no single source suffices — inscriptions, travellers (Paes and Nuniz) and archaeology must be read together.

Worked check: read the founding as strategy — the Sangama brothers, serving under the diminishing Hoysalas, take the Tungabhadra doab in 1336, fortify Vidyanagara (later Vijayanagara, the city of victory), and build legitimacy in two currencies at once: Sanskrit and Telugu titles for the warriors, shrine patronage for the gods (Virupaksha adopted as the royal deity). For the board examination, dynasty questions give founders and year, the Hoysala context, one legitimacy device with an example, and the closing note that the dynasties passed not by revolution but by palace coups and successful generals.

Worked check: tell the succession as four turns — Sangamas rule long and expand; the minister Saluva Narasimha is called to the throne (1485) when the line fails; the Tuluva general Krishnadevaraya raises the empire to its height (1509-29: Orissa warred, Raichur won, Portuguese courted); the Aravidus inherit after Talikota's defeat (1565) and preside over the long unwinding. For the board examination, dynasty-succession answers list the four with dates, one achievement or event per reign (Krishnadevaraya's the compulsory one), and the closing observation that the empire's history is a see-saw between strong ministers-turned-kings and hereditary failure.

Worked check: run the system through one officer — the raya assigns a nayaka a territory (amara) whose revenue supports, say, a thousand horses; the nayaka maintains troops, remits the tribute annually in the Mahanavami's tents, and keeps order locally; his sons inherit only by renewal of the king's favour. Central power stays real because the grant is conditional. For the board examination, amara-nayaka answers define the grant, list the nayaka's obligations (troops, tribute, administration), and close with the double edge — military efficiency in expansion, centrifugal risk when the centre weakened — the standard evaluation the question hunts.

Worked check: read the site like a strategist — Hampi sits in a basin ringed by granite hills, the Tungabhadra guarding the north; boulders give walls without quarrying, hill-crests give watch-points, the river gives water and a border against the Bahmani northwest, and the doab around it is the contested fields everyone wanted. The city is its defence diagram. For the board examination, setting questions ask why here: answer with the four advantages — natural fortification, riverine water and boundary, watch-hills, and the doab's agricultural wealth — and close that geography was the first architect of Vijayanagara.

Worked check: walk the royal centre with purposes in mind — the Mahanavami Dibba, the great earthen platform, where the king reviews troops and receives tribute during the nine-day festival; the hundred-pillared and thousand-pillared mantapas for ceremony and audience; the underground chamber and the aqueduct-fed tanks; the Hazara Rama temple, the king's private shrine whose reliefs tell the Ramayana beside the royal processions. For the board examination, royal-centre answers pair each structure with its function — platform for display, temple for legitimacy, water-works for sustenance — quoting one traveller (Paes on the Dibba's crowds) for the living detail.

Worked check: stage the festival from the sources — on the Mahanavami Dibba the king watches dances, duels, elephants and processions; the twelve chief captains erect their tents of silk on the plain and each presents tribute — horses, gold — which Paes numbers with a traveller's astonishment; the state's hierarchy files past the throne for nine days. Ceremony as audit. For the board examination, Mahanavami answers give the timing, the Dibba as venue, the tribute-and-review choreography from Paes and Nuniz, and the closing interpretation: the festival made the empire visible to itself — power performed annually.

Worked check: trace the sacred axis — the Virupaksha temple, dedicated to the patron deity Pampapati, stands against the river at Mattungi hill's foot, and the royal processional street runs from its gate deep into the city; gods from elsewhere were ritually brought to Virupaksha's court, marriage of deities celebrated with the king as participant. The sacred centre ordered the city's ritual map. For the board examination, sacred-centre answers name the temple and deity, describe the gopuram-and-mandapa additions of the royal phases, explain the processional route's politics, and close that kingship in Vijayanagara was an institution of the god's city.

Worked check: follow the water uphill and down — tanks built in lines along the valleys catch the hill streams (the Kamalapuram tank fed the royal centre's channels and baths); stone embankments store the monsoon; and canals drawn from the Tungabhadra lifted water by devices the travellers describe into the fields. Iron pipe-laid channels ran to the royal bathrooms. For the board examination, irrigation answers give the tank-chain principle suited to the rocky basin, one royal and one agrarian example, and the closing link: water engineering made the doab's rice and the city's gardens possible — the empire drank from its own planning.

Worked check: follow one exchange route — horses from Ormuz shipped to the empire's west-coast ports (Bhatkal), inspected by royal buyers (nayakas needed remounts), paid in the rice, sugar and cloth of the doab's markets; Chinese kalamkari cloth, spices and gems flow out through the same ports to Cambay and the wider world. The Portuguese enter the chain as toll-collectors of the sea. For the board examination, economy answers connect the horse trade (state monopoly's edge), the port taxes, Paes's market scenes, and the closing point that Vijayanagara's wealth was the countryside's grain dressed in a long-distance trade.

Worked check: schedule one agricultural year — kharif sown with the monsoon (rice, cotton, bajra) and harvested in autumn; rabi sown in the cool season (wheat, gram) and harvested in spring; in the canal-rich suba of Punjab and the rice deltas the two overlapped into continuous tillage. Abu'l Fazl's Ain tabulates the crops region by region, which is why the two-season calendar is so precisely recoverable. For the board examination, cropping answers define the two cycles with three crops each, cite the Ain as the source, and close that multiple cropping on irrigated land was the intensification that fed the empire's towns.

Worked check: convene the panchayat in one case — a boundary dispute between fields, a broken irrigation turn, a theft traced to an outsider: the elders hear, judge, fine; the headman (muqaddam) keeps the record and answers the state for the village's revenue; artisans and menials hold service claims (balutas) on the harvest. Village justice before the state's court. For the board examination, village-community answers give the three constituents (cultivators, panchayat, headman), two functions of the council with an example, and the closing caveat: the village ordered itself, but within the empire's revenue demands and the zamindar's shadow.

Worked check: define the two by residence and rate — khud-kashta tills the village he lives in, holds his plot by customary right, and pays the standard assessment; pahi-kashta, an outsider, tills a village he does not live in, pays travelling costs, and takes land on softer terms because the state wants waste brought under plough. Mobility was negotiated, not free. For the board examination, peasant-type answers give both terms with translations (own-resident, non-resident), one reason for each pattern (rights versus incentives), and the closing line that the state courted the non-resident plough wherever land lay idle.

Worked check: itemise one zamindar's powers — his milkiyat: the ancestral land, gardens and beasts he owns outright; his ta'alluqa: the villages whose revenue he collects for the state, keeping his nankar share; his market: cesses on bazaars and passes; his force: cavalry and a mud fort. Three hats — owner, collector, lord. For the board examination, zamindar answers give the definition with the milkiyat-ta'alluqa distinction, the three sources of income, and the closing political reading: the empire ruled through these intermediaries and fought them when they fortified — both halves must be in the answer.

Worked check: read the fort from the revenue rolls — the qila's mud-brick towers and ditch shelter the zamindar's two hundred horse, his matchlockmen and a few elephants; from it he can withhold the harvest, defy a collector, or bargain with a rival raja; imperial armies camp outside and negotiate first, storm second. The stronghold made the zamindar a power, not a taxpayer. For the board examination, military-retainer answers describe the force (composition, sources of pay), the fort's strategic function in revenue resistance, and the closing line that the Mughal peace was punctuated by sieges of exactly such towers.

Worked check: run one jagir through its arithmetic — a mansabdar of 5,000 zat is owed a salary the treasury pays in assignments: he receives a jagir assessed at the matching revenue (jama), keeps what the actual collection yields, and hands over nothing; the diwan reshuffles assignments every few years to prevent roots. If the assessed jama outran the real harvest — in Deccan wars, it did — the jagirdar lost. For the board examination, jagirdari answers give the definition, the salary-for-revenue exchange mechanism, the frequent-transfer rule and its logic, and the closing crisis note: jama-versus-hasil gaps destabilised the system in the eighteenth century.

Worked check: follow one collection season — the zamindar advances loans to his cultivators, collects the assessed revenue in kind or coin after harvest, deducts his nankar and customary dues, and remits the balance to the imperial treasury through the faujdar's oversight; in bad years he bargains the taqavi reduction, in good years he pockets the difference. The state's claim passed through his hands, and stuck there. For the board examination, revenue-right answers describe this chain with the terms (nankar, taqavi), note the checks the state kept (records, treasuries), and close that delegation bought reach at the price of intermediaries' growth.

Worked check: read the field through caste — the plough-caste holds the land; the artisan castes (blacksmith, potter, carpenter) hold service claims on the harvest; the landless labourers work for grain wages; and women's labour, recorded in weeding and harvest, goes unrecorded in the papers. Abu'l Fazl's tables classify peasants by tenure, the village by jati. For the board examination, agrarian-society answers give the three-tier order (caste access to land, artisan baluta service, labouring landless), one evidence each from the Ain or village records, and the closing line that the Mughal countryside was stratified thrice over — by caste, by tenure, by gender.

Worked check: follow grain to market in tiers — the village sells surplus to the travelling beopari at harvest prices; the town's ganj stores it for the months when prices climb; the provincial capital's grain-pasha feeds the city; and the port ships the cotton and indigo out. Cash crops pull the food crops along the same roads, since weavers and towns must eat. For the board examination, agrarian-trade answers give the tiered market structure, one cash-crop example with its export port, and the closing insight from the Ain's price tables: the empire watched grain prices as a matter of state — provisioning was sovereignty.

Worked check: state the crisis as an equation — the assessed revenue (jama) kept rising on paper while the actual yield (hasil) fell behind in the war-torn Deccan; mansabdars pressed for pay, jagirs shrank in value, nobles grabbed the best assignments, and the beggars of the diwan turned to local power: agriculture, taxation and loyalty all frayed together. For the board examination, crisis answers define jama and hasil, give the Deccan context (long wars, famine, noble factions), and close with the eighteenth-century result — jagirdars becoming local rulers, the empire's fiscal spine cracking before its flag fell.

Worked check: fix the settlement's terms — the zamindar is recognised as proprietor of his estate; the revenue demand is fixed forever at a sum calculated (calculated, critics said, too generously) from the 1790s rentals; payment is by sunset rule on fixed dates; default brings the estate to auction. Security of property in exchange for punctual revenue. For the board examination, Permanent Settlement answers give the year, the author and the provinces, the fixity-and-proprietorship terms in two lines, and the debated consequences — investment and stability promised, rack-renting of tenants and the sale of ancient houses delivered — both sides, as the marking scheme demands.
